doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Writing a tune for the Coltrane session
summary: His Brandeis counterpoint exercise, a blues-based tune, was picked up by Coltrane or Dorham and recorded on the spot.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Yes. And I’m very happy to hear that. Do you think of yourself — like many jazz musicians, you’ve worn many hats. Perhaps you were a player first, then you became a composer, in fact you can correct me if this is not right but on that first recording you did with John Coltrane it looks like you had a tune on the record.

Yes and boy that was just something — something that just happened. I had this little extra song. I was doing a counterpoint exercise, and, at the time for my theory class at © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

Brandeis. And I thought okay I’m going to take these two little figures and juxtapose them — and they’re sort of harmonically ambiguous enough that they can go against each other, against changing harmony, they’re kind of non-committal melodically in that sense and I put them one here and one here and one here and one here, I just tried to figure out a way that these two things would fit together and make a little tune. And it was just sitting on my music stand and I don’t remember whether it was John Coltrane or Kenny Dorham or one of the wind players that went, “Oh let’s play this.” That’s how that happened.
When you were working on it did you even conceive it as a jazz tune?
Okay. And then you did a quick arrangement on the spot?

Yeah I mean it was set to a blues so it was nothing to do but play the tune, I’d play blues. So it was easy enough to do. I thought it was awfully friendly of those guys to — you know, older than me, to consider the possibility that this might be something worth doing.
